The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2022-11-10.26.1) introduced by Mayo MP [Rebekha Sharkie](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/mayo/rebekha_sharkie) (Centre Alliance), which means they failed. ### What does this amendment do? Ms Sharkie [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2022-11-10.26.1): > *The purpose of this amendment is to amend section 23 of the Fair Work Act with the effect of changing the definition of a small business. Currently, section 23 defines a small business as a business comprising of 15 employees or less. Casuals are not included in this count unless there is a systematic or regular nature to their employment. For most businesses this would mean most, if not all, of their casual the employees would be included in the employee count for the purposes of defining a small business.* > > *My amendment seeks to change the number of employees that define a small business from 15 to 100. The rationale for this change is simple. Businesses with fewer than 100 staff do not have the human resources departments, they do not have the pay roster, they simply do not have capacity to expend resources—financial and human—to negotiate enterprise bargaining agreements that this bill will potentially force upon them. Without this change we are relegating the thousands of mum-and-dad businesses and entrepreneurial enterprises to an immediate future of costly union-led negotiations. These businesses, many of which are still trying to recover from COVID-19, cannot afford the time or the financial resources.* ### Amendment text > *That the following words be added after the words 90 days: ."; and* > > *(1) parts 1, 2 and 3 of the bill are added to the inquiry; and* > > *(2) calls on the Government to change the definition of a small business from 15 to 100 employees".*

The majority voted in favour of *disagreeing* with [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2022-11-10.38.1) introduced by Warringah MP [Zali Steggall](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/warringah/zali_steggall) (Independent), which means they failed. ### What do the amendments do? The Religious Discrimination (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2021 makes amendments to support the Religious Discrimination Bill, implementing recommendations 15 and 19 of the Religious Freedom Review, establishing a Religious Discrimination Commissioner, and extending complaints-handling to the Australian Human Rights Commission and federal courts. It also amends the Fair Work Act to align with the new religious discrimination protections and includes a contingent amendment to prescribe the Victorian Equal Opportunity Act 2010 if certain Victorian amendments are enacted.

The Human Rights Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 amends Commonwealth antidiscrimination, charities and marriage laws to implement three recommendations (3, 4 and 12) of the Religious Freedom Review chaired by Philip Ruddock. It adds objects clauses recognising all human rights equally, protects charities advocating a traditional view of marriage, and allows religious educational institutions to refuse goods or services for marriages inconsistent with their beliefs.
Financial Services Compensation Scheme of Last Resort Levy (Collection) Bill 2021

The Financial Services Compensation Scheme of Last Resort Levy (Collection) Bill 2021 establishes a levy framework to fund the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort, comprising an annual levy collected from January 2023 and a one-off levy in 2022-23. It gives ASIC responsibility for issuing levy notices, collecting payments, seeking information, and imposing penalties for late payment or incorrect information.
Financial Services Compensation Scheme of Last Resort Levy Bill 2021

The Financial Services Compensation Scheme of Last Resort Levy Bill 2021 was moved for second reading, establishing a levy framework funded by industry entities through an annual levy starting January 2023, with sub-sector caps of $10 million and an overall cap of $250 million, plus a one-off levy on the ten largest financial sector entities in 2022-23 and provision for special levies in response to unforeseen events.
Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response No. 3) Bill 2021

The Financial Sector Reform (Hayne Royal Commission Response No. 3) Bill 2021 establishes a compensation scheme of last resort (CSLR) for consumers with unpaid Australian Financial Complaints Authority determinations, capped at $150,000, and makes amendments to support the new Financial Accountability Regime and transitional arrangements from the Banking Executive Accountability Regime.

The Financial Accountability Regime Bill 2021 extends accountability obligations from banks to the insurance and superannuation sectors, requiring accountable entities to defer at least 40% of variable remuneration for four years and granting APRA and ASIC joint administration and enforcement powers, with commencement from 1 July 2022 for banks and 1 July 2023 for others.

The COAG Legislation Amendment Bill 2021 replaces references to the Council of Australian Governments (COAG) with the National Cabinet and National Federation Reform Council, updating federal structures after COAG ceased in May 2020. The bill also protects the confidentiality of National Cabinet proceedings, reflecting the move to a more agile intergovernmental decision-making model praised by all premiers for its effectiveness during the COVID-19 pandemic.
